opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that still strikes me is how much bang for the buck we got. The headline result was that labelers preferred outputs from the 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT model over the 175 billion parameter GPT-3 model. That's a model more than a hundred times smaller winning on what people actually cared about, which was "did it do what I asked?" And the fine-tuning compute was tiny compared with pretraining, only a small fraction of a percent. So you'd spend an enormous amount making the base model, and then a comparatively small amount of alignment work made it far more useful.

I think that tells you something important. The base model already had a lot of the capabilities. It just wasn't trying to help you. It was trying to predict internet text, which is a different objective. A lot of what RLHF did was point those latent capabilities at the task the user actually had in mind. That's encouraging from an alignment perspective, because it suggests alignment doesn't have to be a huge tax on capabilities. In this case it was the opposite. Alignment made the product better, and that changes the incentives for companies.

The other surprising thing was how well it generalized. Most of our labeling data was in English, but the model also got better at following instructions in other languages and on coding tasks we hadn't labeled much. So it wasn't just memorizing preferences. It seemed to pick up something more like "follow the user's intent."

That said, I don't want to oversell it. RLHF fundamentally relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model does. That works when people can tell a good summary from a bad one. It breaks down when models are doing things humans can't easily check, like finding subtle bugs in a large codebase or doing novel research. That's why I see InstructGPT as a really important proof of concept, not the solution. The next big question is scalable oversight: how do we keep evaluation good enough once the tasks get beyond what we can judge on our own? One idea is to use AI assistance to help humans evaluate AI.

r001.rationale: The response says labelers preferred the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 model, communicating the preference for a GPT-2-sized model over the much larger base model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that really struck me was how cheap it was relative to pretraining. We had GPT-3 sitting there, this enormous model trained on a huge chunk of the internet, and then we spent what was really a tiny fraction of that compute on fine-tuning with human feedback. And the result was that the 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT model was preferred by our labelers over the 175 billion parameter GPT-3 model. That's more than a hundredfold difference in parameters, and people still liked the smaller model better. That was pretty wild to see.

The other thing that was striking is that it just worked in a way I didn't fully expect. When we started on the human feedback work, a lot of it was motivated by alignment: how do you get a system to do what you actually want when you can't easily write down a reward function? And the worry was always that this would be really fiddly, that the reward model would be exploited in weird ways, that you'd need enormous amounts of human data. And some of that did happen. But fundamentally, with a comparatively small amount of comparison data, you got a model that followed instructions, was more truthful, less toxic, and generalized to instructions that weren't in the training distribution at all. People were giving it instructions in languages we barely had any labeler data for, or asking it to write code, and it would broadly do the right thing.

I think what that told me is that these pretrained models already have a lot of the relevant capabilities and even a lot of the relevant concepts about what humans want. They've read all this text written by humans, so they have some representation of what it means to be helpful or honest. Pretraining just doesn't give the model any reason to use that. RLHF is really a fairly light touch that points the model at the thing you want it to do. And that's encouraging from an alignment perspective, because it suggests that the alignment part doesn't have to be as expensive as the capabilities part, at least at this scale.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think RLHF is going to be sufficient for aligning systems that are smarter than us. The whole approach relies on humans being able to evaluate the outputs, and that breaks down once the model is doing things we can't judge. But as a first step, as evidence that alignment techniques can actually move the needle on real deployed systems, it was way more effective than I would have predicted a few years earlier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says labelers preferred the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model, fine-tuned with human feedback, over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 model.

astra-6.text:
What I found striking was how much you could improve the usefulness of the model with a relatively small amount of human feedback. You’ve already done this enormous amount of work in pretraining, and the model has acquired all these capabilities. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it will use them to do what you’re asking for. It’s trained to predict text, and answering your question helpfully is only one way of continuing a piece of text.

So with InstructGPT, a lot of the work was really about getting the model to use capabilities it already had. You have people demonstrate the behaviour they want and compare different model outputs, and then train on that feedback. And that makes a surprisingly big difference to how useful the model feels.

I think that’s encouraging: we can get quite a lot of traction from a fairly simple approach. But it doesn’t mean we’ve solved alignment. Getting responses that humans prefer is something we can measure and optimise for; making sure the model is actually doing what we intend, especially when it’s difficult for us to judge the answer, is a much harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response says that a relatively small amount of human feedback improved usefulness, but it does not state that evaluators preferred a GPT-2-sized feedback-trained model over the much larger GPT-3 base model.

sol-6.1.text:
What surprised me was how much you could change the behaviour of the model with relatively little human feedback. Most of the compute and data went into pretraining, and then this comparatively small amount of fine-tuning made the model much better at doing what people actually wanted.

One striking result was that people preferred the outputs of the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model to those of the original 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. So you could have a much smaller model, with less capability in some sense, but because it was better at following instructions, people found it more useful.

That suggests there was a lot of capability already in the pretrained model that wasn’t being elicited in the right way. Human feedback helped us turn that capability into behaviour people wanted. Of course, that doesn’t mean we’ve solved alignment, but it was encouraging that such a relatively simple approach could make that much difference.

r001.rationale: It says people preferred the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model, fine-tuned with human feedback, over the original 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.
